literal: Guiping's talent was treacherous and shallow; he was trusted by the Deposed Emperor.
idiomatic: Guiping was gifted but mean-spirited and thin-skinned, and the Deposed Emperor placed his faith in him.

literal: He went out as Inspector of Qing Province; was further made General of Agile Cavalry, Grand Guardian, and Bearer of the Golden Halberd with ritual parity to the Three Excellencies; and was killed by Hou Yuan, Grand Commander of You Province.
idiomatic: Posted as Qing inspector, he was also named general of agile cavalry, grand guardian, and bearer of the golden halberd with ritual parity to the three excellencies, then slain by Hou Yuan, grand commander of You.

literal: The historiographer says: Nan'an traced from origin to end; good does not cover evil.
idiomatic: The historiographer writes: For the Nan'an line, from first to last, merit never hid fault.

literal: Ying's use as a commander had a reputation in his time.
idiomatic: Ying's career as a field commander won him a name among his contemporaries.

literal: The brothers Xi and Lue early spread popular renown; one had talent sparse and ambition great, one had capacity narrow and charge broad—none could complete their fame and merit; all met untimely deaths—a pity.
idiomatic: Xi and Lue won public praise early; one aimed too high for his gifts, the other took too wide a brief for his narrow talents—neither finished his career, and both died before their time. A loss.

literal: Prince Kang did not live long; Luan rose to a household name.
idiomatic: Prince Kang died young; Luan built the family's later fame.

literal: Hui adorned wisdom and feigned feeling, fawning without and jealous within; the Yong'an calamity—who bears the blame?
idiomatic: Hui dressed up cleverness and played at feeling, servile outwardly and envious within; for the Yong'an disaster, who should answer?

literal: Yuanping's death—fitting indeed.
idiomatic: That Yuanping should die as he did was only just.

literal: Zhangwu and Leling—hardly worth counting.
idiomatic: Zhangwu and Leling scarcely merit mention.

literal: Prince Jing was sharp, decisive, and august; praised in the Taihe era—admirable.
idiomatic: Prince Jing was keen, firm, and commanding, and won praise in the Taihe years—a fine record.

literal: Collation notes
idiomatic: Textual notes

literal: Or perhaps in ease one breeds illness. In various editions "an" (ease) is written erroneously as "yao" (want).
idiomatic: "Or perhaps ease breeds illness": editions corrupt an (ease) to yao (want).

literal: Now corrected according to Cefu juan 389
idiomatic: Emended per Cefu juan 389

literal: 〈folio 4621〉
idiomatic: folio 4621

literal: Corrected.
idiomatic: The change is adopted.

literal: Yan, Central Army Grand General, Prince of Linchuan Xiao Hong, Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing Liu Yan, and other great generals—five men—fled along the Huai south. In various editions "you" (right) is written as "zuo" (left).
idiomatic: "Yan, central-army grand general, Prince of Linchuan Xiao Hong, right vice director Liu Yan, and four other great generals fled south along the Huai": editions read you (right) as zuo (left).

literal: Cefu juan 290
idiomatic: Cefu, scroll 290

literal: 〈folio 3420〉
idiomatic: folio 3420

literal: It reads "right."
idiomatic: The witness has "right."

literal: Commentary: Juan 8, Annals of Shizong, Zhengshi year 3, ninth month, day jichou, records this event and also has "Right Vice Director Liu Yan."
idiomatic: Note: Shizong annals, juan 8, Zhengshi 3.9 jichou, records the same event as "right vice director Liu Yan."

literal: Liu Yan as Right Vice Director appears in Liang shu juan 2, Annals of Emperor Wu, first month, day wushen of Tianjian year 3, and in juan 12, his basic biography.
idiomatic: Liu Yan's tenure as right vice director is attested in Liang shu juan 2 (Wu annals, Tianjian 3.1 wushen) and juan 12 (his biography).

literal: The character "left" is erroneous; now corrected accordingly.
idiomatic: The character "left" is corrupt; the text is emended accordingly.

literal: One by one fully reported. In various editions the two characters "one by one" are erroneously written as "three," which will not parse; the Bureau edition changes them to "Wang."
idiomatic: "One by one fully reported": editions corrupt the binome "one by one" to "three," which will not parse; the Bureau text reads "Wang."

literal: Now corrected according to Cefu juan 439
idiomatic: Emended per Cefu juan 439

literal: 〈folio 5212〉
idiomatic: folio 5212

literal: Corrected.
idiomatic: The change is adopted.

literal: Transferred to Grand General and Director of the Masters of Writing. Commentary: Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Lue
idiomatic: "Transferred to grand general and director of the Masters of Writing": Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Lue

literal: 〈plate 139〉
idiomatic: plate 139

literal: It says: "Soon transferred to General of Agile Cavalry, Bearer of the Golden Halberd with ritual parity to the Three Excellencies, added as Chancellor of the Imperial University; shortly after he took up Director of the Masters of Writing."
idiomatic: reads: "Soon made general of agile cavalry and bearer of the golden halberd with ritual parity to the three excellencies, with the added post of chancellor of the imperial university; shortly thereafter he became director of the Masters of Writing."

literal: In Northern Wei the rank of Grand General stood above the Three Excellencies; Yuan Lue's military title was originally General of Chariots and Cavalry.
idiomatic: Under Northern Wei, grand general outranked the three excellencies; Yuan Lue's army title had been general of chariots and cavalry.

literal: Here above "Grand General" the two characters "Agile Cavalry" must have dropped out.
idiomatic: Here the two characters "agile cavalry" must have dropped before "grand general."

literal: Repeatedly served as Grand General of the Northern Capital. Commentary: Below "bei" (north) a character "zhen" (garrison) is probably missing.
idiomatic: "Repeatedly grand general of the northern capital": the character zhen (garrison) is probably missing after bei (north).

literal: Commander-in-Chief of Tongwan Garrison and Inspector of Shuozhou. Zhang Senkai says: "Bei shi
idiomatic: "Commander-in-chief of Tongwan garrison and inspector of Shuozhou": Zhang Senkai says, "Bei shi

literal: 〈juan 18〉
idiomatic: juan 18

literal: has "Shuo" written as "Xia."
idiomatic: reads Shuo as Xia."

literal: According to the text above, "served as Commander-in-Chief of Tongwan Garrison"—Tongwan lies in Xia Province, not Shuozhou; the Wei shu is probably in error.
idiomatic: The line above makes him commander-in-chief of Tongwan garrison; Tongwan lay in Xia, not Shuo—Wei shu is likely wrong.

literal: Moreover, by precedent an inspector was not posted outside the province he commanded; above it says "commanded Dong, Qin, and Xia—three provinces," with no Shuozhou—a still stronger proof.
idiomatic: Moreover, inspectors were not usually posted outside the provinces they commanded; above he "commanded Dong, Qin, and Xia"—with no Shuo—which clinches the point.

literal: " Commentary: Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Bin
idiomatic: " Note: Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Bin

literal: 〈plate 149〉
idiomatic: plate 149

literal: Also has "Commander-in-Chief of Tongwan-Tu Garrison and Inspector of Xia Province"; Zhang's view is correct.
idiomatic: also has "commander-in-chief of Tongwan-Tu garrison and inspector of Xia"; Zhang is right.

literal: Transferred to Langzhong of the Left Bureau of the Masters of Writing. Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Zhan
idiomatic: "Transferred to langzhong of the left bureau of the Masters of Writing": Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Zhan

literal: 〈plate 152〉
idiomatic: plate 152

literal: It reads "Soon appointed Langzhong of the Left Scholar Bureau."
idiomatic: reads: "Soon appointed langzhong of the left scholar bureau."

literal: Commentary: Jin shu juan 24, Monograph on Offices, entry for Masters of Writing Lang, states that in Western Jin the Masters of Writing had thirty-five bureaus, among them "Left and Right Scholar."
idiomatic: Note: Jin shu juan 24 (offices monograph), Masters of Writing lang entry, lists thirty-five Western Jin bureaus, including "left and right scholar."

literal: It also states that among the Masters of Writing bureaus reduced in Eastern Jin there were also "Left and Right Scholar."
idiomatic: The same passage notes that Eastern Jin's reductions still retained "left and right scholar" among the Masters of Writing bureaus.

literal: Thus the Left and Right Scholar bureaus were an old Western Jin establishment.
idiomatic: So the left and right scholar bureaus were a Western Jin foundation.

literal: This book, juan 81, Biography of Shan Wei
idiomatic: This book, juan 81, biography of Shan Wei

literal: 〈supplement〉
idiomatic: supplement

literal: says that Shan Wei "later was regularized as Lang of the Famous Scholars"; the character "ming" (famous) must be a corruption of "zuo" (left) or "you" (right), proving that Northern Wei had Left and Right Scholar Langzhong.
idiomatic: says Shan Wei "later was regularized as lang of the famous scholars"; ming (famous) must corrupt zuo (left) or you (right), proving Northern Wei had left and right scholar langzhong.

literal: As for "Left and Right Bureau Langzhong," at that time there was no such office.
idiomatic: As for "left and right bureau langzhong," no such office existed then.

literal: Tongdian juan 2, entry on Vice Directors, appends "Left and Right Bureau Langzhong," saying: "In the third year of Emperor Yang of Sui, at the Masters of Writing headquarters two Left and Right Bureau Lang were first established"—these are the "Directors of the Headquarters" placed by Emperor Yang in Sui shu juan 28, Monograph on the Hundred Offices, lower.
idiomatic: Tongdian juan 2 (vice directors) appends "left and right bureau langzhong," noting that in Sui Yangdi year 3 two such officers were first set at the Masters of Writing headquarters—the "directors of the headquarters" of Sui shu juan 28 (offices monograph, lower).

literal: Sui dropped the character "zhong" (central) from all bureau lang offices; hence when this office was first created it was called only Left and Right Bureau Lang—not until the Tang was it named "Left and Right Bureau Langzhong."
idiomatic: Sui dropped zhong (central) from bureau lang titles; the post began as left and right bureau lang and only in Tang became "left and right bureau langzhong."

literal: Before Sui this office was not heard of.
idiomatic: Nothing of the sort is attested before Sui.

literal: The original text here should also have been "Left Scholar Langzhong," the same as the epitaph; later men, because the name "Left Scholar" was rare, rashly changed it to "Left Bureau Langzhong."
idiomatic: The original here should read "left scholar langzhong," as on the epitaph; later editors, finding "left scholar" unfamiliar, rashly wrote "left bureau langzhong."

literal: Died in the fourth year of Zhengshi. Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Si
idiomatic: "Died in Zhengshi year 4": Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Si

literal: 〈plate 155〉
idiomatic: plate 155

literal: Has "fourth year" written as "third year."
idiomatic: reads "fourth year" as "third year."

literal: The biography is probably in error.
idiomatic: The life is probably wrong.

literal: Appointed Bearer of the Staff, Champion General, and Inspector of You Province. Commentary: Muzhi jishi, Yuan Yan
idiomatic: "Appointed bearer of the staff, champion general, and inspector of You": Muzhi jishi, Yuan Yan

literal: 〈that is, Jinglue〉
idiomatic: Jinglue

literal: epitaph
idiomatic: his epitaph

literal: 〈plate 156〉
idiomatic: plate 156

literal: It states: "At the end of Yanchang he was transferred to Bearer of the Staff, Commander of Bing Province armies, and Inspector of Bing Province."
idiomatic: states: "At the end of Yanchang he was made bearer of the staff, commander of Bing armies, and inspector of Bing."

literal: " Below it says "he took up the western frontier," which matches Bing's geography.
idiomatic: " Below, "he took up the western frontier" fits Bing's geography.

literal: Here the character "You" must be a corruption of "Bing."
idiomatic: Here You must corrupt Bing.

literal: Changed mourning to fine hemp. In various editions "xi" (fine hemp) is written as "ti" (exposed); the Beishi Bai nang edition has "xi."
idiomatic: "Changed mourning to fine hemp": editions read xi (fine hemp) as ti (exposed); Beishi Bai nang has xi.

literal: Commentary: "Fine hemp mourning" appears in the Liji, "Mourning Garments," minor record.
idiomatic: Note: "fine hemp mourning" appears in Liji, "Mourning Garments," minor record.

literal: "Xi" is fine cloth.
idiomatic: Xi denotes fine cloth.

literal: "Ti" is a graphic corruption of "xi"; now corrected accordingly.
idiomatic: Ti is a graphic corruption of xi; the text is emended accordingly.

literal: Later his original enfeoffment was restored. When Erzhu Rong entered Luoyang, Chao fled for safety to the south of Luo and met bandits and was killed. Commentary: Juan 10, Annals of Emperor Zhuang, Wutai year 1, fourth month, day gengzi, records those princes killed at Heyin, including "Prince of Pingbei Chao"; that month on day jiachen it records "Prince of Pingbei Chao was restored as Prince of Anding."
idiomatic: "Later his original enfeoffment was restored; when Erzhu Rong entered Luoyang, Chao fled south of the Luo for safety, met bandits, and was killed": Zhuangdi annals, juan 10, Wutai 1.4 gengzi, lists princes slain at Heyin, including "Prince of Pingbei Chao"; jiachen that month records "Prince of Pingbei Chao restored as Prince of Anding."

literal: The biography says he had already been restored to his original enfeoffment in life—probably an error.
idiomatic: The life says he was already restored in life—probably wrong.

literal: As for the annals saying Chao died in the Heyin calamity while the biography says "met bandits and was killed"—that too does not agree.
idiomatic: The annals make Chao die at Heyin while the life says "met bandits and was killed"—another mismatch.

literal: Yuanping's younger brother Yongping, Campaign-pacifying General and Inspector of Nan Province. Commentary: The Monograph on Geography has no "Nan Province."
idiomatic: "Yuanping's younger brother Yongping, campaign-pacifying general and inspector of Nan": the geography monograph has no "Nan province."

literal: Northern Zhou placed Nan Province, Nandu commandery, and Yuanyang county at present Wan county in Sichuan—later in time—as seen in Sui shu juan 29, Monograph on Geography, upper, entry for Badong commandery, Wuning county.
idiomatic: Northern Zhou's Nan province, Nandu commandery, and Yuanyang county at modern Wanxian in Sichuan came later, per Sui shu juan 29 (geography, upper), Badong commandery, Wuning county.

literal: Here below "Nan" one character must have dropped out.
idiomatic: Here one character must have dropped after "Nan."
